transcript:
>> This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
>> Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Dave Mattingly.
The November midterm elections are four weeks from today,
with polls looking favorable to many Democratic candidates.
President Trump continues campaigning
for Republicans in red states.
He was in Nebraska last night at a rally
for GOP Senator Pete Ricketts.
That's where the president announced he was signing
an executive order to ease restrictions
on the tax-free use of red-dyed diesel.
That's in an effort to bring down energy costs
for truckers and farmers.
AAA says the price of diesel in the U.S.
is averaging almost $6.32 a gallon.
That's about 21 cents off the all-time high set last month.
A new poll out today shows Democrats have a nearly two
to one edge over Republicans
when it comes to voter trust on health care costs.
NPR's Selena Simmons-Duffin reports.
>> The cost of health care is weighing heavily on voters'
minds with the midterm elections just one month away.
That's according to the new poll from KFF,
a nonpartisan health research organization.
KFF's Ashley Kurzinger says they polled
1,300 people in mid-September.
>> What we are seeing is that the Democratic Party
has the advantage overall among all voters
on which party voters trust to handle health care,
but they also have the advantage among independent voters,
and that's a really important voting block
for midterm elections.
>> Kurzinger says Democrats had a 10-point advantage
on health costs in April.
Now that gap has doubled.
22% of voters trust Republicans on the issue
compared to 42% who trust Democrats.
Selena Simmons-Duffin, NPR News, Washington.
>> President Trump says he and his super PAC
will begin paying for TV ads
that have been taxpayer-funded up to now.
NPR's Frank Ordonez says those ads
have prompted pushback from Democrats.
>> President Trump announced the new plan
amid ongoing backlash over the publicly funded spots
running ahead of the midterms.
Trump defended the ads via his social media page,
arguing that it was standard practice,
and that he was promoting the USA
and, quote, "paying for them with USA money."
But critics say the pro-Trump ads are blatantly partisan
and use Republican talking points.
Trump says that he and his political action committee
are taking over payment of the ads.
Franco Ordonez, NPR News.
>> A former U.S. Army major
convicted of a deadly shooting at Fort Hood, Texas,
17 years ago, will be executed by firing squad.
President Trump has approved that method of execution
for Nadal Hassan.
In November of 2009, Hassan opened fire at the Army base,
killing 13 people and injuring more than 30 others.
Hassan later said he was trying to prevent American soldiers
from being sent to Afghanistan to fight the war on terrorism.
This is "NPR News" from Washington.
Health officials in Pennsylvania say the state
has surpassed 1,000 cases of measles this year.
It marks the largest outbreak in any state in the U.S.
in more than three decades.
Nationwide, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
says there have been nearly 3,900 reported cases in 2026.
Pennsylvania reports five measles-related deaths this year.
In addition to the Keystone State,
large measles outbreaks have been reported in Texas,
Utah, and South Carolina.
Attorneys general in New York and Illinois
are making fraud allegations against a company
that helps U.S. military veterans
qualify for disability benefits.
Trajector Medical charges vets as much as $20,000 each
for help that prosecutors say is supposed to be free
under federal law.
NPR's Chris Arnold says this follows an NPR investigation.
-The AG say one thing that they're investigating
is the company's use of a robo-dialer system
that we uncovered in our reporting.
It calls the VA and poses as the veteran
so it can send bills to thousands of vets.
That's even if Trajector didn't actually help them
to get disability pay.
-We also now know that Trajector made nearly $280 million
in income just last year.
Dustin Ingram is a former Army Ranger and combat vet
who felt taken advantage of.
-It's a mind-blowing amount of money.
It's inconceivable that somebody made that much money.
Like, there's a problem somewhere in the system, right?
-Trajector told NPR in a statement, quote,
"We stand behind how we operate
and we're focused on the veterans we serve."
Chris Arnold, NPR News.
I'm Dave Mattingly in Washington.
-Wanna hear this podcast without sponsor breaks?
Amazon Prime members can listen to NPR News Now
sponsor free through Amazon Music.
Or you can also support NPR's vital journalism
and get NPR+ at plus.npr.org.
That's plus.npr.org.

topics.text: President Trump signs executive order easing restrictions on tax-free red-dyed diesel for truckers and farmers
New poll shows Democrats have two-to-one edge over Republicans on voter trust in health care costs
President Trump announces he and super PAC will begin paying for TV ads previously taxpayer-funded
Former U.S. Army Major Nadal Hassan convicted of 2009 Fort Hood shooting will be executed by firing squad
Pennsylvania surpasses 1,000 measles cases this year, marking largest outbreak in any state in over three decades
Attorneys general in New York and Illinois allege fraud against Trajector Medical for overcharging military veterans for disability benefits help
